title: Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS)
subtitle: The standard envelope for signing, sealing and authenticating data of any kind.
summary: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is a general container format for protecting data. One wrapper, ContentInfo, names a content type and carries it, and the type can be a digital signature, an encrypted envelope for one or more recipients, a plain digest, a password-style encryption with no recipients, or a message authentication code. Wrappers can be nested, so a message can be signed and then encrypted. It descends from PKCS #7 and is the foundation of S/MIME email.

plainLanguage.summary: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) is a general container format for protecting data. One wrapper, ContentInfo, names a content type, such as a digital signature, an encrypted envelope for recipients, a digest or a message authentication code. Wrappers can be nested, so a message can be signed and then encrypted. CMS descends from PKCS #7 and underlies S/MIME email.

tldr.problem: Programs that sign or encrypt data each invented their own file format, so protected messages could not be read by other software.
tldr.mechanism: A single ASN.1 wrapper, ContentInfo, labels its contents with an object identifier and can hold signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data or authenticated-data, and these wrappers can be nested.
tldr.outcome: One common format carries signatures and encryption for S/MIME and many other protocols, with the choice of cryptographic algorithms left to other documents.

today: CMS is everywhere that standard signatures or encryption on a blob of data are needed. S/MIME secure email builds on it (see RFC 8551), as do time-stamp tokens, and signed and sealed objects in many other protocols. The OpenSSL command-line tool has an openssl cms subcommand for creating and reading CMS messages, and libraries such as OpenSSL, Bouncy Castle and Windows CryptoAPI can parse it. Two later documents extend this one: RFC 8933 adds protection for algorithm identifiers and RFC 9629 adds key encapsulation mechanisms (KEMs) as a key management option.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) describes how to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt arbitrary message content. The RFC calls it "an encapsulation syntax for data protection". An encapsulation can sit inside another, and one party can sign data that someone else has already wrapped.

CMS values are defined in ASN.1 and encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER). The syntax supports certificate-based key management, such as the PKIX model in RFC 5280, and it lets extra attributes, for example a signing time, be signed along with the content.

CMS began as PKCS #7 version 1.5, an RSA Laboratories note from November 1993 that is republished as RFC 2315. The IETF then took over. RFC 2630 put it on the Standards Track, RFC 3369 added password-based and extensible key management, and RFC 3852 added extensible certificate and revocation formats. This document obsoletes RFC 3852 mainly to advance CMS up the maturity ladder, and it folds in the multiple-signer clarifications from RFC 4853.

CMS defines the container, not the cryptography. Specific algorithms are left to other documents, such as RFC 3370, so each can be updated on its own schedule.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS describes how to digitally sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt any message content. One protected item can sit inside another, and one party can sign data that someone else has already wrapped. Extra attributes, such as a signing time, can be signed along with the content.

sections.title: The Wrapper and the Six Content Types
sections.content:
Everything in CMS starts with ContentInfo, a SEQUENCE of two things: a contentType, which is an object identifier, and the content itself, tagged [0] EXPLICIT. The identifier says how to read the content. The RFC defines six types: data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-data.

An implementation MUST implement ContentInfo and MUST implement the data, signed-data and enveloped-data types. The other three MAY be implemented. New content types can be defined outside this document, and if they are, the ASN.1 type SHOULD NOT be a CHOICE.

The data type is just an arbitrary octet string whose meaning is left to the application. S/MIME uses it for MIME-encoded content. The other types wrap data or each other, so a plain message might be signed (signed-data wraps data), then encrypted (enveloped-data wraps signed-data).

Each type is designed for single-pass processing with indefinite-length BER, which helps when the content is large or is piped from another process. The one exception is that signed attributes and authenticated attributes must be DER encoded, so a recipient can verify content that has attributes it does not recognise.
sections.plainLanguage: Every CMS message starts with ContentInfo, which holds a content type identifier and the content itself. The identifier says how to read the content. There are six types: data, signed-data, enveloped-data, digested-data, encrypted-data and authenticated-data. Implementations must support the first three.

sections.title: Signed-data
sections.content:
Signed-data holds content of any type plus zero or more signatures. Any number of signers can sign in parallel. To build one, each signer computes a message digest of the content, signs the digest with a private key, and packs the signature with other signer information into a SignerInfo. Certificates and CRLs may be added, and the whole is collected into a SignedData value.

A SignerInfo says which certificate to use through a sid, which is either an issuer name with a serial number (version 1) or a subject key identifier (version 3). Receivers MUST accept both forms. It also names the digest and signature algorithms and may carry signedAttrs.

If signed attributes are present, the digest that gets signed is computed over their DER encoding, using an explicit SET OF tag rather than the [0] tag. They MUST include a content-type attribute and a message-digest attribute, so the content is protected indirectly. The signedAttrs field MUST be present whenever the content type is not id-data.

Omitting eContent gives an "external signature" where the content travels separately. The recipient MUST NOT trust any digest the sender computed, and must recompute it. Where several signatures are present, a valid one from a given signer is usually treated as that signer's signature, though an application can set other rules.

The RFC warns about compatibility with PKCS #7. CMS carries content as an OCTET STRING, while PKCS #7 allowed a variable ASN.1 type, so digests can differ when the content is not of type data.
sections.plainLanguage: Signed-data holds content plus any number of signatures. Each signer computes a digest (a short fingerprint) of the content and signs it with a private key. The signature goes into a SignerInfo that identifies the signer's certificate and the algorithms used.

sections.title: Enveloped-data
sections.content:
Enveloped-data is encryption for one or more recipients. The sender generates a random content-encryption key, encrypts the content with it, then encrypts that key separately for each recipient and stores each result in a RecipientInfo. A recipient decrypts their copy of the key and then the content. The same content-encryption algorithm and key serve every recipient.

The RecipientInfo CHOICE supports five key management techniques, shown in the grid. Implementations MUST support key transport, key agreement and previously distributed key-encryption keys. They MAY support passwords, and may support any other technique through ori. Unknown alternatives must be handled gracefully.

The recipientInfos field comes before encryptedContentInfo so a value can be processed in a single pass, and there MUST be at least one recipient. When an algorithm needs input in blocks of k octets, the data is padded at the end with k minus (length mod k) octets, each holding that value. Input that already fits is still padded, so removal is unambiguous. This works only for k below 256.
sections.plainLanguage: Enveloped-data encrypts content for one or more recipients. The sender creates a random key, encrypts the content with it, then encrypts that key separately for each recipient. Each recipient decrypts their copy of the key, and then the content.

sections.title: Digested, Encrypted and Authenticated Data
sections.content:
The remaining three types cover narrower jobs. Digested-data is content plus a message digest of it, so a recipient can check integrity by recomputing the digest. It is typically used as input to enveloped-data. Its version is 0 when the content type is id-data and 2 otherwise.

Encrypted-data is encrypted content with no recipients and no encrypted keys at all, so "Keys MUST be managed by other means." The RFC's typical use is encrypting data for local storage, perhaps with a key derived from a password. Its version is 0, or 2 if unprotectedAttrs is present.

Authenticated-data carries content, a message authentication code (MAC), and the MAC key encrypted for each recipient with the same RecipientInfo machinery as enveloped-data. If authenticated attributes are present, the MAC is computed over their DER encoding, and the digest algorithm field MUST also be present. Version is 0, 1 or 3 depending on which certificate types appear in originatorInfo.

When more than two parties share a MAC key, no one can tell which of them made a given MAC. Any holder of the key can produce a valid one.
sections.plainLanguage: Three narrower types remain. Digested-data is content plus a digest, so a recipient can check integrity. Encrypted-data has no recipients, so keys must be managed by other means. Authenticated-data carries content and a message authentication code (MAC), with the MAC key encrypted for each recipient.

sections.title: Useful Attributes
sections.content:
Attributes are labelled extra values attached to a signature or MAC. An Attribute is an object identifier and a SET of values. Where an attribute appears matters: signed and authenticated attributes are covered by the signature or MAC, while unsigned attributes are not.

Section 11 defines four. The content-type attribute repeats the type of the content being protected, and the recipient checks that it matches eContentType. The message-digest attribute holds the content's digest and MUST be present whenever any signed or authenticated attributes are. Both MUST be signed or authenticated, never unsigned, and each must have exactly one value.

The signing-time attribute records when the signer (purportedly) signed. Dates from 1 January 1950 to 31 December 2049 MUST be encoded as UTCTime, as YYMMDDHHMMSSZ, and other years as GeneralizedTime. The RFC imposes no requirement on whether the time is correct; accepting it is up to the recipient.

A countersignature is a signature on another signature. It is an unsigned attribute whose value is a SignerInfo, computed over the signature value of the signature it countersigns. It MUST NOT contain a content-type attribute, and countersignatures can themselves be countersigned in an arbitrarily long chain.
sections.plainLanguage: Attributes are extra labelled values attached to a signature or MAC. Signed attributes are protected by it, and unsigned ones are not. The content-type and message-digest attributes must be signed. The signing-time attribute records when the signer claims to have signed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of CMS rests on keeping keys secret. Compromise of a signer's private key permits masquerade. Compromise of a key management private key or key-encryption key may expose everything protected under it, and compromise of a content-encryption key exposes that one message. Compromise of a MAC key allows undetectable modification.

Weakest link
When one key encrypts another, the effective strength is the weaker of the two. The RFC's example is a 168-bit Triple-DES key wrapped with a 40-bit RC2 key, which gives at most 40 bits of protection.
MAC origin
The key management used for authenticated-data must itself provide data origin authentication. RSA and ephemeral-static Diffie-Hellman do not. Static-static Diffie-Hellman does, if both public keys are bound to identities in certificates.
Randomness
Content-encryption keys, MAC keys, IVs and padding must be randomly generated, and weak generators can make keys easy to guess. The RFC points to RFC 4086.
Countersigning
Countersigning covers only the signature value, so a countersigner could sign an inappropriate signature. Verify the original first, or countersign only in a context that ensures this.

Algorithms weaken over time, so implementations should be modular and ready for the required set to change.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS security depends on keeping keys secret. A stolen signing key allows impersonation, and a stolen key-encryption key may expose everything protected under it. When one key encrypts another, protection is only as strong as the weaker key. Keys, IVs and padding must be generated randomly.

children.label: digestAlgorithms
children.note: SET OF DigestAlgorithmIdentifier, may be empty

items.title: ktri: key transport
items.text: The content-encryption key is encrypted in the recipient's public key. Version 0 with issuerAndSerialNumber, 2 with subjectKeyIdentifier. MUST be supported.

items.title: kari: key agreement
items.text: The sender's private key and the recipient's public key derive a pairwise key, which encrypts the content-encryption key. Version always 3. MUST be supported.

items.title: kekri: pre-shared key
items.text: The content-encryption key is encrypted with a symmetric key-encryption key distributed earlier. Version always 4. MUST be supported.

items.title: pwri: password
items.text: The key-encryption key is derived from a password or other shared secret. Version always 0. MAY be supported.

items.title: ori: other
items.text: An object identifier names a technique defined in a future document. MAY be supported, and unknown ones must be handled gracefully.
